pedagogy.summary: The nth-term (position-to-term) rule expresses the structure of EVERY term directly from its position, so you can jump to the 100th term without listing. For an arithmetic sequence it is (common difference)×n + (zero term): the coefficient of n IS the constant difference, and the constant is the 'zeroth term' one step before the first. The nth term is new learning at KS3 and must be built from — and sharply distinguished from — the term-to-term rule, which only tells you how to get the NEXT term. Fluency means deriving it, using it to reach far terms, and testing membership by solving a linear equation.
bestPractices: Build the rule from growing shape / matchstick patterns so the coefficient of n is SEEN as the repeated group and the constant as the fixed starting part; rewrite terms to expose structure (4 = 1+3, 7 = 1+3+3, 10 = 1+3+3+3)
State explicitly that the coefficient of n equals the common difference, and that the constant is the zeroth term (step back one before the first term) — not the first term
Use the shared sentence 'As the value of n increases by one, each term increases (or decreases) by ___' to tie the difference to the coefficient of n
ALWAYS verify a proposed rule by substituting n = 1, 2, 3 and checking it regenerates the actual terms
Plot the terms and read the common difference as the steepness, but do not join the points (non-integer positions have no meaning)
Test membership by setting the nth term equal to the target and solving the linear equation, accepting the number only if n is a whole number
Deliberately include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences so the rule generalises beyond positive-integer, increasing cases
keyRepresentations: Growing shape / matchstick patterns (the repeated group = coefficient of n, the fixed start = constant)
Position-vs-term table with an explicit '0th term' column
The 'as n increases by one, the term changes by d' sentence frame
Plotted terms on a graph (steepness = common difference; points not joined)
'Set the rule equal to the target and solve' for membership testing
commonMisconceptions: Uses the common difference as the WHOLE rule: writes n + 4 (or just 'add 4') for 3, 7, 11, 15 instead of 4n − 1
Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — assumes a sequence going up by 3 must contain multiples of 3
Whole-object method: finds the 100th term by taking the 10th term × 10, or claims the 10th term is twice the 5th (only true when the line passes through the origin)
Gets the sign wrong for decreasing sequences: writes 4n + 6 for 10, 6, 2, −2 instead of −4n + 14
Attends to the term-to-term rule instead of position, so cannot reach a far term without listing
Over-generalises from only-increasing examples, treating decreasing sequences as a different kind

learn.summary: Learners derive and apply the nth-term (position-to-term) rule for an arithmetic sequence, sharply distinguishing it from the term-to-term 'add d' rule. The core structure: the coefficient of n is the common difference, and the constant is the 'zeroth term' one step before the first term (not the first term itself). Fluency means deriving the rule from structure, verifying it by substituting n=1,2,3, jumping to far terms (e.g. the 100th) without listing, and testing membership by solving rule=target and accepting only whole-number positions. Include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences so the rule generalises.

activities.title: Build the rule from a growing pattern
feedback: If a learner writes n + 4 (or 'add 4') for 3, 7, 11, 15, have them substitute n=1,2,3: it gives 5, 6, 7, which steps by 1 and starts wrong. Contrast with 4n (right step, wrong start), then adjust the constant to reach 4n − 1.

If a learner writes 4n (forgetting the −1) or 4n + 3 (using the first term as the constant), point out that 4n gives 4, 8, 12 (each value 1 too big) and 4n+3 gives 7, 11, 15 (the real terms shifted one position along). Step back before the first term to find the zeroth term: 3 − 4 = −1.
Reinforce: the constant is the value at n = 0, found by going one step before the first term, not the first term itself.
activities.rationale: Building the coefficient as a seen repeated group and the constant as a stepped-back zeroth term ties each part of the rule to visible structure; the NCETM guidance links the coefficient to the common-difference meaning and documents the n+3-instead-of-3n+1 error that this derivation targets.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; the coefficient of n represents the common difference (as n increases by one, the term increases by that amount); documented misconceptions include writing n+3 instead of 3n+1, confusing 'multiples of three' with 'increases by three', the whole-object method (100th term = 10th term ×10; 10th = twice 5th, only valid through the origin), and wrong sign for decreasing sequences (4n+6 for 10,6,2,−2).
learnerActions: Work through an illustrative growing shape or matchstick example such as 4, 7, 10, … and rewrite each term to expose structure: 4 = 1+3, 7 = 1+3+3, 10 = 1+3+3+3. Here the fixed start 1 is the zeroth term and the repeated +3 is the coefficient, giving the rule 3n + 1.
Apply the same technique to the target sequence 3, 7, 11, 15: identify the repeated group (+4) as the coefficient of n and the fixed starting part (the zeroth term) as the constant.
Find the zeroth term by stepping back one step before the first term (for 3,7,11,15: 3 − 4 = −1), and state the rule as 4n − 1.
Complete the sentence frame 'As the value of n increases by one, each term increases (or decreases) by ___' and connect that difference to the coefficient of n.
activities.intendedInsight: The nth-term rule reads structure directly from position: the coefficient of n IS the common difference, and the constant is the term at position zero — found by stepping back one before the first term, not the first term itself.

activities.title: Position machine: test a rule and jump to far terms
feedback: Always verify a proposed rule by substituting n=1,2,3 and checking it regenerates the actual terms before trusting it.

For a decreasing sequence, if a learner writes 4n + 6 for 10, 6, 2, −2, note the coefficient of n is the signed difference: a decreasing sequence needs a negative coefficient (−4n + 14). The wrong rule may give the first term by luck (4×1+6 = 10) but fails at later positions (4×2+6 = 14, not 6) — substitute n=1,2,3 to catch it.

Live interaction examples (optional, not required): drag an n slider to assemble each term as n copies of a difference-block on a fixed start-block; a 'test all' button that lights cells green/red; a 'jump to n=100' button. These make the mechanism concrete but are not the only way to run the activity — a table or pencil-and-paper substitution works just as well.
activities.rationale: Substitution-based verification and leaping to a far term directly target the whole-object misconception and the habit of attending only to the term-to-term rule; the signed-coefficient check addresses the documented wrong-sign error for decreasing sequences.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; the coefficient of n represents the common difference (as n increases by one, the term increases by that amount); documented misconceptions include writing n+3 instead of 3n+1, confusing 'multiples of three' with 'increases by three', the whole-object method (100th term = 10th term ×10; 10th = twice 5th, only valid through the origin), and wrong sign for decreasing sequences (4n+6 for 10,6,2,−2).
KS3 national curriculum requires pupils to 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term' and to generate terms from a position-to-term rule.
learnerActions: Type a candidate rule into a 'test all' box that substitutes n=1,2,3,4,5 and marks each term green (matches the real sequence) or red (does not).

Watch a wrong rule fail visibly: n+4 turns every cell red (it gives 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 instead of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19), while 4n−1 lights every cell green — so the term-to-term rule and the position rule are seen to differ, not just told apart.
Use a 'jump to n=100' control to produce the 100th term instantly (399 for 4n−1) and feel why listing is absurd.
Repeat the derive-then-verify cycle for a decreasing sequence (10, 6, 2, −2 → −4n + 14) and a decimal/fraction sequence so the rule generalises beyond increasing positive-integer cases.
activities.intendedInsight: A position rule can be tested against the real terms and used to leap straight to any position; a rule written as 'n + d' from the term-to-term 'add d' rule generally fails substitution, and the coefficient carries the SIGNED difference, so a decreasing sequence needs a negative coefficient.

activities.title: Membership testing by solving an equation
feedback: If a learner judges 101 to be in the sequence because it is odd like the real terms, do not reteach the whole concept — scaffold the method: set 4n−1 = 101 and solve; a term exists only when n comes out a whole number.
Emphasise that surface features (odd/even, 'looks similar') are not evidence of membership; only the solved whole-number position is.
activities.rationale: Solving rule=target with a whole-number-position check directly replaces surface-judging of membership — the performance error flagged in the source material. This uses the KS3 position-to-term rule but is an inverse application not asserted by the cited claims, so no source claim is attached.
learnerActions: Given a target number, set the nth-term rule equal to it and solve the linear equation for n.
Accept the target as a term only when n is a whole number; reject it when n is non-integer.
Work the deliberately misleading case: for 3,7,11,15,… test 101 by solving 4n−1 = 101 → 4n = 102 → n = 25.5 → not a whole position → not a term; then test 99 → n = 25 → yes.
When a target is rejected, find the nearest actual terms (99 at n=25 and 103 at n=26) to show which values really belong.
activities.intendedInsight: Membership is decided by solving rule=target and checking for a whole-number position, not by whether a number 'looks like' the others (e.g. being odd).

activities.title: Graph the terms and read the difference
feedback: If a learner claims the 100th term equals the 10th term × 10 (or the 10th is twice the 5th), use the plot: doubling the position does not double the term unless the graph passes through (0,0). Use the position rule and substitute instead.
Remind learners not to join the plotted points: only whole-number positions exist, so a continuous line would imply meaningless in-between terms.
activities.rationale: Plotting ties the coefficient to steepness and exposes why the whole-object/multiply-a-term method fails except through the origin; the 'do not join points' caution preserves the integer-position idealisation.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; the coefficient of n represents the common difference (as n increases by one, the term increases by that amount); documented misconceptions include writing n+3 instead of 3n+1, confusing 'multiples of three' with 'increases by three', the whole-object method (100th term = 10th term ×10; 10th = twice 5th, only valid through the origin), and wrong sign for decreasing sequences (4n+6 for 10,6,2,−2).
learnerActions: Plot the sequence terms against their position numbers.
Read the common difference as the steepness between successive plotted points, and connect this to the coefficient of n.
Do NOT join the points with a line — positions are whole numbers, so non-integer positions have no meaning here.
Use the graph to challenge the whole-object claim: check whether doubling the position doubles the term, and notice this only holds if the plotted line would pass through (0,0).
activities.intendedInsight: Steepness on the position-term graph matches the common difference, and multiplying a term's value in step with its position only works when the line passes through the origin.

activities.title: Check and consolidate fluency
feedback: For membership items, require the solved whole-number position before accepting an answer; a number that merely resembles the sequence's terms is not thereby a member.

A static annotated card (coefficient highlighting the repeated +4 group; tap/reveal the 0th term) is a useful summary reference, but on its own it does not let a learner test a candidate rule against the real terms — use it after learners have derived and tested rules themselves.
activities.rationale: Recognition and selected-response items efficiently check fluency and surface specific misconceptions (n+4 vs 4n−1, whole-object, surface-membership); by design they verify recognition rather than elicit independent construction of the rule, so they follow the building activities.
learnerActions: Complete fill-the-blank items (e.g. 'nth term of 3,7,11 is __n__') and choose between distractors that pit n+4 against 4n−1.
Answer a multiple-choice item whose distractor is the whole-object claim '100th term = 10th term × 10', explaining why it is wrong.
Decide a membership item where the target (e.g. 101) is odd but not in the sequence, so surface-checking fails and only solving succeeds.
Use a labelled reference card: the sequence with +4 arrows, the rule 4n−1 annotated, and the zeroth term revealed (3−4 = −1) as a consolidation summary after the main work.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recognise the correct position rule, reject the whole-object shortcut, and settle membership by solving rather than by appearance.

constraints: The nth term is new learning at KS3 and must be built from — and sharply distinguished from — the term-to-term rule, which only gives the next term.
State explicitly that the coefficient of n equals the common difference and the constant is the zeroth term (one step back before the first term), not the first term.

Keep any term decomposition consistent with its own sequence: 4=1+3, 7=1+3+3, 10=1+3+3+3 illustrates 4,7,10,… (rule 3n+1, zeroth term 1); for 3,7,11,15 the repeated group is +4 and the zeroth term is 3−4=−1, giving 4n−1.
Always verify a proposed rule by substituting n=1,2,3 before accepting it; a rule that gives the first term correctly can still fail later (common for wrong-sign decreasing cases).
Deliberately include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences; the coefficient of n is the SIGNED difference, so decreasing sequences have a negative coefficient.
Membership must be decided by solving rule=target and accepting only a whole-number position, never by surface features such as parity or resemblance.
When plotting, read steepness as the common difference but do not join the points — non-integer positions have no meaning.

A static annotated diagram is a consolidation/reference scaffold: it does not let a learner test a wrong rule against the real terms or independently jump to a far term, so it should follow, not replace, derivation and verification.
Recognition/selected-response items check fluency but do not elicit independent construction of the rule; use them after building activities, not instead of them.

Live-manipulation features (sliders, test-all lights, jump-to-n, membership solver) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete but are optional; equivalent work can be done with tables, graphs, and pencil-and-paper substitution.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited claim (DfE KS3 Mathematics programmes of study, position-to-term requirement) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight accordingly.

The candidate had merged the difference-3 decomposition (4=1+3, 7=1+3+3, 10=1+3+3+3) into the difference-4 sequence 3,7,11,15, which contradicted its own stated rule 4n−1 (the decomposition implies start 1 / rule 3n+1). This is corrected by presenting 4,7,10,… as a distinct illustrative example before applying the technique to 3,7,11,15.

The membership activity previously cited the DfE position-to-term claim; membership-by-solving is an inverse application not asserted by either source claim, so its sourceClaims has been set to [] with the KS3 link kept only as context.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: for 3,7,11,15 the rule 4n−1 gives 3,7,11,15 (correct); zeroth term 3−4=−1 (correct); 100th term 4×100−1=399 (correct); 101 → 4n−1=101 → 4n=102 → n=25.5 (not a term), 99 → n=25 (term). For 10,6,2,−2 the rule −4n+14 gives 10,6,2,−2 (correct); the distractor 4n+6 is wrong and is used only as an error to catch, never as a valid option. For 4,7,10,… the rule 3n+1 gives 4,7,10,13 (correct), zeroth term 1. All checked consistent.
The non-preferred 3D entry's claim that rendering a flat concept in 3D 'adds no depth' was treated as a catalog preference, not a universal law, and omitted rather than asserted.

The source framed the 2d interactive as 'ideal' and the static image/quiz/conversation as weaker; these fit rankings were removed and the useful content from each (reference card, assessment items, Socratic 'convince me 4n−1 not n+4' challenge) was preserved as distinct activities.

probeDeeper: Your rule is 4n − 1. Show me where the −1 comes from — what is the term at position zero?
Without listing, how do you know the 100th term? Convince me that finding the 10th term and multiplying by ten would NOT work here.
If the sequence had been 10, 6, 2, −2, … instead, what would change in your rule and why?
You said 101 is not in the sequence. What is the nearest number that IS in it, and how did you find it?
assess.correctAnswer: nth term = 4n − 1; 100th term = 399 (4×100 − 1); 101 is NOT a term because 4n − 1 = 101 gives n = 25.5, not a whole-number position (the terms either side are 99 at n=25 and 103 at n=26).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the common difference as the whole rule: writes n + 4 (or 'add 4') for the nth term because each term goes up by 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them substitute n = 1, 2, 3 into n+4 and see it starts at 5 and steps by 1; contrast with 4n (right step, wrong start) then adjust the constant to −1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Their rule gives 5, 6, 7, … at n = 1, 2, 3 rather than 3, 7, 11 — but they typically do not substitute to check

errorPatterns.pattern: Right coefficient, wrong constant: writes 4n (forgets the −1) or 4n + 3 (uses the FIRST term as the constant instead of the zeroth term)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find the zeroth term by going back one step before the first (3 − 4 = −1); the constant is the term at n = 0, not the first term
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 4n gives 4, 8, 12; 4n+3 gives 7, 11, 15 (off by one position) — they never step back to the zeroth term

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-object / multiply-a-term: finds the 100th term by taking the 10th term and multiplying by ten, or claims the 10th term is twice the 5th
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plot the terms — doubling the position does not double the term unless the graph passes through (0,0); use the position rule and substitute
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Their 100th term does not match the rule's value; the method only works when the line passes through the origin (0,0)

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong sign for a decreasing sequence: for 10, 6, 2, −2 writes 4n + 6 (difference read as +4) instead of −4n + 14
errorPatterns.nextMove: The coefficient of n is the SIGNED difference; a decreasing sequence has a negative coefficient; verify by substituting n = 1, 2, 3
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rule generates the first term correctly but not subsequent terms; they treat the difference as positive because they see '4' between terms

errorPatterns.pattern: Decides membership by how the number looks (it is odd, or 'looks like the others') instead of solving the rule = target equation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach the concept: set the rule equal to the target and solve; a term exists only when n comes out a whole number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 101 is in the sequence without solving; performs no whole-number-position check

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a position rule; continues by adding 4 repeatedly and would list all 100 terms to reach the 100th; decides membership by how the number looks.
responseLevels.full: Derives 4n − 1 explaining coefficient = common difference and constant = zeroth term, jumps to the 100th by substitution, settles membership by solving 4n−1 = 101 → n = 25.5 → not a whole position → not a term, and transfers the method to a decreasing or decimal sequence.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 4n − 1 and the 100th term by substituting, but treats it as a remembered procedure — cannot say why the coefficient is the common difference or the constant is the zeroth term, and reverts to listing or surface-judging when the sequence decreases or when membership is asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … Find a rule that gives you any term straight from its position number, and use it to work out the 100th term without listing them all. Then tell me: is 101 in this sequence — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the position-to-term structure writes 4n−1, reaches the 100th by substitution, and settles membership by solving to a whole-number position. A child who only has the term-to-term rule cannot get the 100th without listing, tends to write n+4 or 4n, and judges membership by surface features. The target 101 is deliberately ODD (like every real term) so 'the terms are odd and 101 is odd, so yes' fails — only solving 4n−1=101 reveals n=25.5. And n+4 versus 4n−1 diverge immediately at n=1 (5 vs 3), so the wrong rule is caught the moment it is checked.
